p: This question is for ACS. How many college students do you have in the system? Because to me, that number is still low based on the amount of students that's in care?

Right, so between the ages of 18 to 21, if you look at that as college age, we have 745 youth in care. Of those youth, we have 471 this semester in College Choice. However, they don't all attend CUNY, they attend different schools, as I mentioned.
And what kind of support do they have when they attend a school outside of the CUNY system?

So if they attend school outside of the CUNY system, they continue to get um, their case planning offered by the foster care agency. They're eligible for a Fair Future Coach, so they continue to work with them. Maybe it has to be remote, but there's still expectations that visits and support, and that they're making connections with those that

are around them, um, at their university. Let's say they're going to University of Albany. We're also working very closely with New York Foundling. They won the RFP award for our College Choice Support Services Program, CCSP, um, and in that they help us support the payment process for, you know, the bursar's bills and all of those things, but also provide additional support to the young person— academic advisement, if they need a tutor, they'll make sure that they're connected to social-emotional programs. Sometimes our youth will continue with therapy. So New York Foundling provides that added layer of support. So we put that in place to support our young people, you know, wherever they're attending school.
And they also provide housing because I did see a great housing for foster age— foster youth.

So the youth that when they go to care— when they go to care, they're in care when they go to school, excuse me, um, we work with them to identify what is the place, best place for them to live. So some will live in a dorm setting. Some

universities have their own housing, but it's off campus. They may decide to live there. Some young people stay within their foster care placement. So we work with them, but we do provide support. College Choice pays up to $30,000 a year in housing.

Um, we understand that funding is allocated to campuses based on the number of eligible FYSCI students who are enrolled, thus allowing funding to follow the student. How does CUNY Central Administration ensure that FYCSI programming and supports are consistent and of equal quality across CUNY campuses?

So because the funds are held centrally, we send the funds to each campus based upon the number of students that they have. And so that way we can ensure that funding is at the campuses for the students that are there. Um, so we have campuses with large numbers of students that most of the funding would be there, and we have some campuses with smaller numbers of students, so less of the funding is there. But then we track the funding and we ensure that the funding gets to the student and their tuitions are paid and they're getting their FYCSI awards as well.
And if a student decides to attend a SUNY school, how do you work together with the SUNY school to provide the same level of support?
So for FYCSI, um, because FYCSI is at the SUNY schools as well, I will— we'll call our counterparts or we'll call OCFS and say this student is transferring to Albany.
Mhm.
And so then they'll— they were found eligible at Baruch, but now they're transferring to Albany. And so they'll know that the student is eligible at Albany and they'll put the student up there.
With the same level of care?
For FYCSI. Uh, this— the individual SUNY school, if I'm not mistaken, will provide the supports that they provide to the schools. They don't centralize their program the way CUNY does.
Yeah, I know they do have a foster, a foster youth program. I just wanted to see if there was overlap and if there's collaboration between the two systems.
Yes.
Um, what dedicated staff offices or point of contact exist on CUNY campuses to support students who've been in foster care? How different are they from campus to campus?

So we have, um, I sit centrally, but I work with the financial aid and Bursar's offices to identify the students and make sure they know who their students are. And from time to time, I'll also work with, for example, the level— the Office of Student Affairs at the individual campuses when, um, we need to continue or to, uh, increase the level of support for a student. Um, so it would depend on the campus, but the larger campuses have the, the most number of students, and so we're most in contact with them as well.
And how often do you meet to go over trends that you're seeing in the system or little hiccups that you're seeing in the system? How often do you meet?
With the—
With the campuses.

With the campuses? So I meet with the campuses regularly, and I'm always in

communication over email because that's how we get the funding out.
Okay. Um, what is the retention rate for students receiving FY— FYCSI support? What has been the trend in retention rate for students who receive services over the past 5 years?

So the retention rate has gone up as our— as our numbers have gone up as well. Um, like I said, we are— our data folks are still working on the actual retention numbers, and we can give that to you later. But the retentions have— the retention is going up, and everything is trending upwards, as with our graduation rates.
Yeah, we want to make sure young people are getting the support and staying. And if they don't, how do you go back and do outreach to get them back?

So we'll— we check, uh, registration for students both, um, several weeks into the fall, several weeks into the spring and over the summer, and we'll regularly reach out to students who are not, who are not registered for that semester

to let them know that we'll be here when they come back or if they decide to come back.
And how do you remove some of— if they tell you, hey, I have a— this is the issue, how do you support that?

So it depends. Usually the issues are financial, so students will have a, uh, like a bursar hold because they owe money at a school. And so one of the things that we do at CUNY that we make sure happens is that we remove- we can cover past balances, prior balances. So if a student can't attend school because they owe funds at either that same school that they want to come back to or a different school, I will get in touch with whichever one it is, the school, to say the student is coming back. We need to remove the hold so that they can register, and then we'll cover the past balance and any current balances that might— because of the instability sometimes about foster youth, sometimes they are the first to go to college and don't have that support. Um, so therefore that's why we asking how much support is provided and when they do fall through the cracks sometime, how— what is— what does that

outreach look like? How do we get them back? Whether it's, um, any, any, um, programming. Because we want to make sure our foster youth are graduating as well. We don't want them just to go to college to go to college, but we want them to also graduate, have meaningful lives. Um, so what's the graduation rate for students receiving FY, um, CSI support, what has been the trend in graduation rates for students who receive services over the past 5 years?
So-
And I'm gonna— and I'm gonna add another piece to that. Once they finish, is there support in helping them find pathways to careers?

So approximately 31%— so our trends for graduation are going up. Approximately 31% of all students served over the past, um, 10 years have, have already completed a degree. And as I said before, some have completed multiple degrees. What we also try to do, because with the support of our social work interns, that case management, we connect students who are coming out of college. So we are working with them to see what their next step is, if it's a job, if it's graduate school, um, and

we try to make sure that they're connected post-graduation with our program. But FYCSI stops at the bachelor's level, but we try to make sure when they come out they've got some support.
Is that with um, career, career advisement, um, internship placement if necessary. Certain fields require internship, apprenticeship, mentorship. Is all that included in that as well?

Yes. So we have programming that's specific to careers, for example. So we'll send out information throughout the year, even not just to students who are graduating, because the student might step out and need a job. Um, so we're always sending out information to students around careers, making sure students know the resources that are available to them in those ways, connecting them to their career counseling centers at the CUNY campus as well, because that's the— you know, they do a really good job of supporting our students in that.
Is that also with resume writing and-?
Yes interview skills.
Mock interview skills. Okay, I'm gonna pass it over to Council Member Stevens, and then I'll come back.

Hello, good morning. Um, I just had a follow-up question, um, because the numbers that you gave, I just wanted to know around the program, um, and for the colleges. I see like, um, BMCC has like 188 students, but like your college has 7. Is there like— do each college do like its own recruitment? Um, have— is there a reason why there's like inconsistencies? I see like everyone else is kind of like more around the same, but those two were just kind of glaring to me. Just wanted some clarification.
We learn of our students once they're already generally at the college. So we don't work on like where do they go to school. Once they've applied, then we'll, we'll know who they are. So I'm not— I—

Are you guys like seeing any trends? Is it because more of them are like in the city or they have better pro— like, yeah, is that like— because I'm just wondering, like, if we see that, you know, a lot of folks are going to BMCC,

like, what are they doing that like something like your college could do? And are we looking at those trends or even considering it? Is it that like maybe it's too far or whatever? I don't— I'm not sure. I just would love for us to, like, think about that, of thinking, like, okay, well, what— why is there such a big difference?

I will— I usually— sometimes I'll work with the admissions offices to see if they want us to come in and have presentations around FYCSI for students, because it's also about knowing that there are foster youth there as well. And I don't know that they're, you know, what, what the outreach is for foster youth at the campus. So we'll do that sometimes as well. And that's also something that we've looked at, um, but the trends— I, I, I think that BMCC is also one of our bigger community colleges, so that might also be why the numbers are higher there as well.

Yeah, I would just love for us to like kind of think about that and make sure that like maybe there— some schools are not as nice or they're not as welcoming, right, or have the information as available. Like, I think that there's

probably something there we should look into it. Nothing— it's bad, maybe it's something good, maybe just BMCC, or you like it there, I don't know, just thinking. I just was looking at the numbers and that just kind of glared out to me. SHIRLEY DE PENA; Yes.
Um, I guess, um, these— some of the questions are for ACS. Over the past 5 years, how many youth have aged out of foster care annually, and what percentage of those youth were enrolled in college?

Thank you for your question. So I'll break it down year by year, and then I can give you the total numbers so you can see the trends. So in 2021, 533 youth aged out of care, 79 were in college. 15%. In 2022, we had 500, um, youth aging out of care. 90 were in college, 18% overall. 2023, 429 youth aged out of care. 68 were in college, which was 16%. In 2024, 382 aged out of care. 82 were in college, 21 per— which was 21% of the population. And in 2025, 358 youth aged out of care. 84 were enrolled in college, which is 23%.

So we are seeing that the number of children aging out of care is going down, which is a data trend we like. And we're also seeing that the percentage going to college is increasing. Yeah, small steps, but we're getting there.

Baby steps. It's all you could ask for. How, um, how are, um, eligible students informed about the programs such as College Choice, FYCSI, and Fair Futures, and what steps are being taken to increase awareness and participation?
So for the kids in care, um, we do a lot of work obviously with our foster care providers. They are doing all of the case planning.
Mhm.

So we hold a lot of information sessions. Sonia and her team, and she can talk a little bit more, will talk to agency case planners. Agencies have educational specialists. They have what we call preparing youth for adulthood, which is a specialist that really focuses on building into independent living skills. If we know children are not being adopted, going home, or Kin Gap. We really wanna prepare them for their adulthood.

So agencies have these, um, key point people. So they're educated around College Choice, the requirements, what it looks like. Um, we also work, as I mentioned, with the, with the case planners, and then agencies have Fair Future coaches. They're responsible for hiring their coaches. We partner with the Center for Fair Futures who provides the training and the technical assistance. So all of this information about College Choice, our workforce development programs, our summer youth employment, um, are communicated with these professionals, and it's their responsibility to engage young people. We also have a very close relationship with the foster care office at New York City Public Schools. Um, in terms of the flyer about, um, FYSE, um, fostering FYCSY, we do have that. We share that information with them and also about College Choice. So we do a lot of outreach, a lot of, um, um, information sessions, providing information to providers to make sure they're aware of how, um, you can get young people into College Choice and then the benefits.

I am positive that we're gonna have young people testify today that there is

inconsistencies. And even with all that effort that you just explained, that they're still not getting the information. And so what are we doing? Because I know when I had a roundtable, young people suggested, like, not just relying solely on the providers of, like, how do we get this information to them directly? Because um, even when we had a roundtable, I remember that they started doing case management with each other and telling each other about the programs because every agency ain't the same. And so how do we get to a place where the consistency is across the board and that young people can also access it without, you know, always having the barrier of the, the agency who often does not do the legwork that these young people— and, and, and the reality is even was there, I was like, well, clearly y'all should just be working in the agencies because y'all doing the job right now. Like, I mean, literally giving up— like, no, you didn't know you're eligible for a laptop? Oh, you should go here. Oh, let me give you this website. And that— and there's young people like, what are you talking about? I don't know what you're talking about.
So that's, you know, not what we want to hear, but we can always do-
Positive.
No, no.
So many heads shaking back there, and I think— and they're all going to come testify after to say yeah.
And I would love to hear more, you know, about like which agency for the youth that are currently in care and, and how they get the information.
I'll tell you, I promise you.

No, I'm not— no, I, uh, absolutely. So one of the things we do, we do have at ACS the Youth Leadership Council. So for example, on Saturday they're having what we call a hype event. This is a youth-led information forum. We've invited all the youth in care to come to this event. We're going to have information about College Choice Fair Futures. So I think what you're— based on what you're saying, I think we need to hold more of these types of events because it's youth, like, the youth are

talking about the programs and, and how to get more information. And maybe we need to leverage some other, um, tools, maybe social media, our website that we can share information.
It's terrible. It's not good. It's no, it's not good. It's not good. If I was a young person, I wouldn't go in there. And I'm old and I'm like, it's terrible. So, yeah.

So, so we're gonna work on those things, um, and, um, and we'll, we'll coordinate with Stephanie and maybe we'll have the Youth Leadership Council. They can give us some information about— maybe, maybe they could help us monitor it. So anyway, but I think those are the, um, the ways to make sure that youth have the information directly, and that way we're not relying on if there's a, uh, uh, somehow there's a gap in, in—

Yeah, one of them suggests that, um, like having some type of app that young people can just download and have access to all the information. But it's the city and we don't believe in technology, so I was just like, that's probably not gonna happen. So we know technology is terrible in the city.

So yeah, we did look at creating— well, that's another story. We did look at creating an app at one point and it didn't get to where we wanted to, but I think, um, there's been some, um, easement in how to use social media. And so we'll look at that and then we can talk to the young people about what might be a way to share information. And many agencies have different types of youth forums, and we can make sure that we're sharing that information with those that host the youth forums.

I'm sure they're gonna give us suggestions when they come up to testify, so just be ready to take some notes, 'cause I, I take notes. I don't— listen, young people do my social media. How, um, how are eligible students informed about program— oh, I asked that. What, um, formal communications and coordination and mechanisms exist with CUNY and ACS to identify, track, and support students, um, with foster care experience while they are enrolled in CUNY institutions?

So in terms of kids that are in College Choice, and Sonia can talk more about her relationship with, with CUNY, one of the things we do when children are accepted into College Choice, we

ask them to apply for all of the different, um, programs, scholarships, financial aid. So if you're in foster care, you're going to be enrolled in the, um, FYCSI program and then Sonia has— and working with New York Foundling, we have a database, so we're able to track every student and where they're going to school. And then there's constant conversation and types of follow-up. So that's how we kind of continue to work together. So if, you know, young people are struggling and maybe they need some additional support, we're able to make— reach out to the agencies and get that information, um, to the kid and get the young person the services they need. But Sonia can talk more about the coordination.
Mhm. Good afternoon— morning.
Yeah, something.

Hi, we're here. Um, I mean, Shirley and I coordinate consistently on the students who are enrolled at, uh, in College Choice and at CUNY. Um, we actually just had a conversation this morning on the way up about a student that we need to support today. Um, but through our application process, um, just like Ina said, we make sure that

students are applying for the grants and scholarships that they're eligible for, particularly FYSE. We ask them to submit the, er, proof of enroll— proof of application to FYSE to make sure that they can access those benefits. And that opens up the doors for resources and the collaboration for us to ensure students are connected to the resources at CUNY. But then also if there are other issues that arise, we work closely with the provider agencies, their coaches, their specialists to make sure that concerns are addressed timely. Um, whether it's social-emotional, whether it's housing, whether it's academic, um, um, supports that are needed. We also, as you know, you heard several times, we have New York Foundling, who is a support service provider, and they are also our, our ears on the ground, our boots on the ground. They support our students, um, who are in college, just helping them to navigate that complexity of, um, being in foster care and also being at a higher education institution.

Since ACS launched the College Choice program in 2022 and expanded in 2025, what metrics are being used to evaluate program

success, like enrollment, persistence, graduation, um, and employment outcomes? Are there plans to future expand the program? And if so, what is the anticipated timeline and scale of that expansion?

So since the program started in 2022, we had 200, um, youth in care, and now this semester we have 471. So we definitely are tracking enrollment. We're also tracking persistence, and I believe that in terms of children that continue, 75% of those young people continued on. We've had 9% of our students that are enrolled in CUNY graduate, which was 27. And then, um, the remaining students we continue to support. Overall, we see about a 30% dropout rate, which somewhat aligns with kind of, you know, normal— not normal, but outside of foster care populations. Excuse me. Um, we continue to also track, like, the type of school, um, they are attending, their GPA. It's very important that we pay attention to the GPA. And then also looking at, um, the length of time it takes them to complete their degree. Sonia, are there any of the other data elements we track— and we have a huge database.

You mentioned, um, enrollment, persistence, and graduation rates are the, the baseline metrics that we track in College Choice. Um, we also track the graduation status and what we don't necessarily on a long-term basis track where are they employed. But because we offer them the post-grad stipend for 6 months after graduation, and they have to apply for that post-grad stipend, um, once they graduate and provide their diploma and their final transcript, we do track wit ]
Stipend.
$60 a day.
Oh.
So $60 a day for 7 days a week. And our graduates get that for 6 months after graduation.
Like the counsel.

Um, and so our students do, on the application, tell us what their plans are for after graduation. So some of them are going to grad school, some of them are going employment, some of them are, um, you know, embarking on internship opportunities.
Yeah, it's a good way to make people come back and stay connected.

Wait, just so— just to piggyback, you asked about expansion, plans for expansion. So when the program started, it was funded at around $10 million this fiscal year, fiscal year 2026, we were able to increase the funding to $15 million, like $15.6 million, and then we will baseline $18.7 million in fiscal year '27. So we are going— the goal this year was to serve 430. We exceeded that goal, but next year we'll be budgeted to serve up to 530 kids, if not more. And because of how the funding works, and depending on the scholarships and the financial aid need, we can sometimes support more children within the budget because one child may not have as-
As much—
Right, exactly.
Yeah, understood. Um, what percentage of foster care youth who enroll in College Choice programs attend a CUNY institution, and what are the percentages of— and graduation rate of those students?
It's 63% of the children that are currently in College Choice attend a CUNY school.
I have more questions, but I'll pass it over so we can not talk about it. Yes, okay.
Um, Council Member Epstein.

Thank you, Chairs. Um, and thank you all for being here. Um, so, Ms. Wallace, can I ask you a couple of questions? So, um, it'd be good to know from your experience of this process, 'cause going through it, um, kind of what your experience was. Um, so, you know, I know you mentioned getting your GED. How, how was that process? Were there people there who helped you along the way? Like, what were the barriers that you experienced to get your GED?

Um, yes, so when first, um, gaining my GED, it was very difficult. I think I failed the math like twice, um, by 5 points because you would need 500 to actually go on. Um, but it wasn't until I got into like college when I got my GED where I started to see like resources and support for academically.
So you— if you had gotten support resources earlier -
If I had — oh my gosh, yeah, I'd get a high school diploma, a certificate, I'd get you everything I could.
And, and applying to college, what pro— what was that process like for you? Like, just making the decision to apply. Did you get support in that process when you were applying to college?

Um, so when I got to Gram Slam which is, um, like for alumni in the foster care system. They, um, they gave me different alternatives. Like, they didn't, like, budget me in and say, you can't go to— like, um, I remember Alex and Shirley constantly— I kept saying, I want to go to Hunter. Now, mind you, I'm in Queensborough Community College, but I'm gonna go to Hunter. And I always felt like that was more of a prestige school than I wouldn't. But surely enough, Shirley and Alex didn't lie. I got into Hunter, and I'm there right now. So I think, um, with that support and just constant— because again, like you guys said, like,

um, Chair Steven said, you know, that you— when you don't have that support or someone kind of letting you know, um, hey, this is where you go, FIC has this, Shirley's here, uh, Chair Joseph, Chair Epstein has this— when you don't have those, someone directly telling you, you don't know. So it was really great to come into that program and they kind of just opened my horizons to so many things. I no longer felt like I had to stay at Queensborough Community College. I was so much more, like, um, determined and I felt so much more confident when going to school because I was going to a school that I actually wanted to go to. So—

So just if I can ask one more question. So just to think through the gaps that we're just trying to feel like it, 'cause we're worried about young people like you falling through these kind of, these gaps. Um, it seems like there were moments like applying for the GED, getting connected to people. How did you find it? Like, how did those connections work for you? Just someone told you, hey, college is possible, think about this program, you can get tuition support? Like, how did that work for you in your life?

Um, I, I think, um, one, one way was definitely I had great social workers around me, so they were always someone that was, um, like, that I looked up to. But mainly, um, having— like I said, being able to receive laptops, being able to receive, um, transportation, having my coach reach out to me, um, every once a week and say, hey, McKeema, I just wanna know, are you, you know, you know, we have these things going on. Do you know that this is here?
Mhm.

Um, a lot of the things that, a lot of the information that I did receive was because of a, a coach that was provided to me by— I will be honest with you, Chair, um, Epstein, I did not receive the full educational services I deserved. Until I got into FYC— FYCSI. FYCI. I, I'm sorry, I'm all— yeah, um, so it, it was literally— and, and I'm not just saying that, uh, like I said, I had Graham Slam prior when getting my GED, and I failed that about twice. I had to kind of do that on my own. It wasn't— and I, I did that because I wanted to get into the dorm project. I wanted to go to school.

So they told me, hey, if you get your GED, if you get your high school diploma, we can connect you to that. So that was like my big determination because I knew once I got there, then housing stability, everything else I needed would fall into line as far as just surviving and being able to do my education.

Do you think other kids in foster care get that information? Because obviously what you're saying is really important. Like, you saw there was a future for you because you saw college as a pathway forward. Do you think other kids in foster care know that this is available to them, or, or when are they—

I'm gonna be honest with you, um, Chair Epstein, a lot of them, uh, don't. I've met, like, and not because Shirley isn't, most of the time, especially when you're coming from that environment of not having a support system of school constantly or repetitively, it's like you, you have to try to find your own way. And luckily we have, like, we have students like myself or others or like for me, when Shirley would come out to the schools and talk to us about it, that was something that gave me the insight.

Um, like she says, they have QR— uh, QRO codes now. So anytime I see something, especially that says foster youth, knowing that I'm in foster care and I press it, it's a— it's very easier to like apply, get the information. Um, something that I wish that I did have in like ACS, like the Graham Windom, was my FYC aside coach and Shirley. I felt like if I may have had them in my beginning stages for high school wanting to go to college, it would have been different because she has already painted that picture afterwards. But can you imagine before if I got to meet her? So, um, that's something that I, I really pray and hope that one day, foster care agencies, do allow them to come do— come speak to the high schoolers. Not, you know, when they just get to college, but before then, because that's going to make them want to go. I wanted to be, like I said, a social worker. And that was enough for me to see her with her button-up shirts and her cool outfits, and that was enough for me. That was it. So I, I, I think if others got that insight, it would, it would help a lot.

So if I could just jump in, everything she, um, Ms. Wallace is saying is really important. It's one of the reasons why we started the Fair Futures program in 2019. And so for young people ages 11, they get a— they get a tutor, they have access to tutoring, and the program is also designed to provide a coach starting at 14. And the coach is a little more on the ground— soon you use the term boots on the ground, um, in terms of like speaking with a young person. It's a mentor, not a mentor. So maybe it's like, oh, I'm interested in playing basketball, they'll connect you. Um, and so these are newer programs, um, that we're growing and over 4,300 young people in 2025 got a coach. But I think the coach can do some of those things and help bridge the gap, spread more— spread information about college or just anything, like, if you're interested in anything else. And so I think, um, I don't think that when you were around that 14-year-old age, I don't know if they had the Fair Future coach yet, but that's, that's kind of like how we stepped up to meet that type of gap.

And Ms. Peña, can I just— one last question if I can. So obviously we have an amazing young person here, and I'm wondering, are there— are you worried there are other young people who are falling through the cracks who are coming into the program or not getting access to the program or applying, getting turned down from the program, that those gaps that are missing to be able to help?

I do, I’m sorry, I often worry about gaps, um, just because I know it's, it's natural, right? We can send an email, people don't read emails. We can send— so there's, there's naturally going to be gaps, and I do worry about that, which is why I try to think like, what are all of the different kinds of ways that we can do the same thing? One of the things that struck me a couple of years ago, I regularly send out emails. McKeema can tell you, I just send out emails and, and people don't read, like, people don't respond, you know, students don't respond. And I, and-
I experienced that too.

So, so, you know, I just said, okay, but, but one summer a student needed help and it's a student that had never responded to any of my emails and they called me because they needed help at their campus. And they were like, I don't know if you know me. And I'm like, I know you. Absolutely, I know you, and I helped them. And what it— what it told me in that moment was that even though they didn't respond to my email, they read it maybe, or just knew, like, you know, maybe it was like, I don't need whatever Shirley's talking about today. But they knew who Shirley was, they knew who FYCSI was. And so one of the things that we do with our social work interns, um, you know, sometimes things come to me because somebody does a really good thing and I'm like, oh my God, that's your job from now on. So we had a social work intern write a monthly email to their caseload of students and they said, oh, you know, happy October. And I said, you know what? That's a really good idea because what I learned over the summer is that even when they don't respond to you, they are reading the emails.
